4a58881c03:
The guide scopes this domain to four things: error types, recovery strategies, trace analysis, and isolating integration-layer problems from model-output problems. This chapter covers each in turn:

  • one taxonomy that covers transport, HTTP, capacity, validation, tool execution and model-output failures;
  • a map from each class to the recovery that can actually fix it (retry with backoff and jitter, fallback models, repair prompts, circuit breakers);
  • what to log per agent turn, and how to read a multi-turn trace;
  • a procedure for "is it our code or the model?", built from replay, fake clients, prompt diffs and deterministic checks.

Three end-to-end incident case studies then apply the whole method: a nightly job losing work to 529s, an agent looping on a failing tool, and JSON failures after a model upgrade.
5b43c90606: Neighbouring chapters: chapter 05 owns the full HTTP status table, the SDK's built-in retries and the rate-limit headers. This chapter points to it rather than repeating it. Chapter 06 covers errors inside a stream, chapter 07 failed batch items, chapter 18 structured outputs and defensive parsing, and chapter 21 tool error design.
194ee6ae2e:
A Claude integration fails in two places with different physics: the integration layer (network, HTTP, quotas, request shape, your parser, your tools) fails deterministically and is fixed in code or config, while the model's output fails statistically, as a well-formed 200 that is truncated, refused, off-format or wrong, and is fixed in the prompt, tools, schema or model choice and then measured over many runs.

Debugging is the discipline of deciding which layer a symptom belongs to before choosing a fix, using recorded traces, replay, fake clients and deterministic checks, because a retry cannot fix a bad request and a prompt rewrite cannot fix a truncation bug.
a05620193e:
At 2.6% of 53 items, the domain gets one or two direct questions. But the reasoning shows up inside many others.

The typical stem describes a symptom ("intermittently returns half a JSON object", "the agent keeps calling the same tool", "it got worse after the deploy") and offers four fixes. Usually one distractor is a model-quality fix for an integration bug: use a bigger model, add "be careful" to the prompt. Another is a retry for something a retry can't fix. A third is plausible but treats the symptom. The right answer names the layer.
407d40c057: Nothing in the recovery half of this chapter is new. It's the standard distributed-systems toolkit, applied to one more remote dependency. What is new is the second failure physics. Most of the skill lies in knowing which ideas carry over unchanged and which don't.
2b199015bf: Classify before you retry. HTTP itself (RFC 7231 and successors) splits 4xx, "the client is wrong", from 5xx, "the server is wrong". Every mature RPC stack since has encoded the same rule: only some failures are worth repeating. gRPC status codes, for example, separate UNAVAILABLE (retry) from INVALID_ARGUMENT (don't).
b9a8902654: Backoff with jitter. Ethernet's binary exponential backoff (1970s) solved collisions on a shared wire. Each station waited a random slot from a doubling window. The same idea came back to service clients with Marc Brooker's 2015 AWS Architecture Blog post. He showed that pure exponential backoff still produces synchronised retry waves. "Full jitter" (a uniform random delay up to the exponential ceiling) spreads them out, at little cost in completion time.
1c904da636: Circuit breakers. Michael Nygard's Release It! (2007) named the pattern. After repeated failures, you stop calling a dependency for a cool-down period and fail fast. That way a slow or dead dependency can't consume every thread in the caller. Netflix Hystrix popularised it on the JVM. Resilience4j is its maintained successor, and probably what your Spring services already use.
53b4650277: Tracing. Google's Dapper paper (2010) introduced the trace/span model. Every unit of work carries a trace id. Each hop records a span with timing and attributes, and the spans reassemble into a tree. OpenTelemetry standardised it. Its generative-AI semantic conventions define span attributes for model name, token usage and finish reasons. They're still evolving, so check the OpenTelemetry docs for current attribute names.
4876bd82be:
What is new. Every tool above assumes that a successful response is a correct response. A language model breaks that assumption. An HTTP 200 can carry output that stops mid-sentence, declines the task, violates your schema, or calls the wrong tool. And the same request may succeed on the next attempt for no reason you can see.

This second failure physics needs two additions to the toolkit. First, check every successful response before trusting it. Second, measure failure rates over repeated runs instead of reproducing a single failure.
b434a3372e:
The integration layer is everything you wrote or configured: the HTTP client and its retry settings, the request builder and prompt templates, the model id, the parser that reads content, the tool dispatcher and the tools themselves.

Its failures are deterministic. Given the same input and the same recorded response, your code fails the same way every time. That's good news. A deterministic failure can be reproduced offline and pinned with a unit test.
38ebe53f53:
The model-output layer is the content of a successful response. Its failures are statistical. A prompt that returns valid JSON 97 runs in 100 has a 3% format-failure rate, and no single rerun tells you whether a change helped.

You fix these by changing what the model sees: instructions, examples, tool descriptions, schema, model choice, max_tokens. Then you measure the rate again, over enough runs to tell the difference.
723dcf464f: The boundary matters because the fixes aren't interchangeable. Rewriting a prompt won't fix a parser that reads content[0].text when the first block is a thinking block. Retrying won't fix a schema the model misreads 5% of the time. It just pays for the misread twice. The most expensive debugging sessions are the ones where a team works on the wrong side of the line for days.
ac04aaa568: A useful taxonomy maps each class to exactly one first response. Chapter 05 lists every HTTP status the API documents and whether to retry it. Here those statuses collapse into a few classes, and we add the classes that never produce a status code at all.
bf686c280f:
Two things in the table are easy to miss.

First, quota is not capacity. A 429 with a retry-after header means "slow down". The errors page says a tier spend-cap 429 has no retry-after and keeps failing until access resumes. A retry loop that treats both the same will spin for hours against a monthly cap.

Second, the bottom three rows produce no HTTP error at all. Generic error handling (an exception filter, a Spring @ControllerAdvice, an alert on 5xx rate) sees a healthy service while users get truncated answers. Those classes need checks that your code runs on every successful response.
85cc0250fc:
A table of classes is easy to memorise and hard to apply. Real failures arrive as log lines and user complaints, not as class names.

So this section takes one realistic incident per class from a telecom customer-care deployment: a billing assistant, an outage assistant and a ticket-opening agent, all sharing one Claude gateway service. Each incident is worked the same way. What was observed? Which evidence settles the class? What's the instinctive wrong fix, and what's the fix that holds?

The point of doing it eight times is to make the reasoning automatic. Look for a status code. Then look for the header or body detail that splits the class. Then check the precondition of the recovery you're about to apply.
062af0b2d2:
Observed. After a network change, about 4% of requests from the outage assistant fail with APIConnectionError. The rest succeed. The failures cluster on requests with long outage reports attached.

Evidence. There's no HTTP status and no request-id, so the request never got a response from Anthropic. The failing requests are the large ones. And the failures started with the network change, not with a code or prompt change.

Classification. Transport, integration layer. The model never saw these requests, so nothing about prompts or models is relevant.
0825e038ea:
Wrong instinct. Raise the SDK's max_retries. Retrying a connection error is safe, since no response means no side effect at the API. It will also mask the problem for a while. But a deterministic, size-related drop at a proxy fails on every retry and multiplies latency by the retry count.

Fix that holds. Find the hop that drops the connection. The usual suspect is a corporate egress proxy with a body-size or idle-timeout limit. Fix its limit, and keep the default retries for genuinely transient blips. The distinguishing test is cheap: replay one failing request from a host that bypasses the proxy. A transport failure that tracks payload size or duration is configuration, not flakiness.

A related variant, APITimeoutError on long generations, has a different fix: stream the response. The errors page recommends streaming for long requests. A streamed response keeps the connection active and returns partial progress, instead of one long silent wait.
389b0184d5:
Observed. A deploy at 14:02 sends every billing request to a 404 not_found_error.

Evidence. The status is 4xx, and the failure rate jumped from 0% to 100% at a deploy boundary. The response body names the resource. The rendered request shows "model": "claude-sonnet-5.5", with a dot where the id uses a hyphen.

Classification. Request error, integration layer, deterministic.

Wrong instinct. A fallback chain that catches "any error" and moves to the next model. It would serve everything from the fallback model, the dashboards would show green, and the typo would live for weeks.

Fix. Correct the id. Add a startup check that sends one tiny request per configured model, or validates ids against the models list endpoint (check the docs for its shape). And make fallback code re-raise 4xx.

The same reasoning covers 400 invalid_request_error for malformed turns, 401 for a revoked key, 403 for a key without access, and 413 request_too_large. The errors page sets the Messages API body limit at 32 MB. It notes that on the direct API the 413 comes from Cloudflare before the request reaches Anthropic, which is why a 413 has no Anthropic request id in the body. A 413 is usually a base64 image or PDF that should have gone through the Files API (chapter 06).
a53776405b:
Observed. Every weekday at 09:00, when a batch of overnight tickets is re-opened, 429 rate_limit_error rises to 15% for ten minutes.

Evidence. Each 429 carries a retry-after header of a few seconds. The anthropic-ratelimit-* response headers (chapter 05) show output tokens per minute at zero remaining just before the burst.

Classification. Capacity. The request is fine; the rate isn't.

Wrong instinct. Retry immediately with more workers.

Fix. Honour retry-after, which the SDKs already do. Smooth the burst with a queue that admits work at the tier's rate. If the overnight re-open job doesn't need interactive latency, move it to the Batch API (chapter 07). The errors page also warns that sudden usage spikes can trigger acceleration-limit 429s, and it recommends ramping traffic up gradually. A job that goes from zero to full concurrency at 09:00 is the textbook case.
132dcfcaab:
Observed. On the 28th of the month, every request fails with 429. The retry wrapper keeps each job alive for an hour before giving up, and the job queue backs up.

Evidence. These 429s have no retry-after header. The errors page says exactly this about the usage tier's monthly spend cap: it has no retry-after and keeps failing until access resumes. Retrying won't help.

Classification. Quota. The same symptom with HTTP 400 instead of 429 is the organisation or workspace spend limit you configured yourself. The errors page routes that one to invalid_request_error (except for a Claude Code workspace, which returns 429). And 402 billing_error means a payment problem on the account.

Fix. Classify missing-retry-after 429s as quota. Stop retrying, page the owner, and fail jobs into a resumable queue. Add a spend forecast alert at 80% of the cap, so this becomes a planning conversation rather than an incident.
08e65b2f37:
Observed. A handful of 500 api_error responses per hour, with no pattern by prompt or customer.

Evidence. 5xx status. Each body carries a request_id. The same requests succeed when retried.

Classification. Server, transient.

Fix. The SDK's default retries already absorb this. What's left for you is to log the request_id and to alert only if the rate rises above its baseline. The errors page says to include the id when contacting support; Python and TypeScript expose it as _request_id on responses. 504 timeout_error belongs here too, with the streaming advice from the transport case.

One special case: an error event inside a stream that already returned HTTP 200. The errors page is explicit that standard status handling doesn't catch these. A streaming consumer must treat the event as a failure of the whole response and discard the partial text (chapter 06).
c49eb95213:
Observed. The refund classifier emits "action": "refund_full" in about 1% of outputs, and the downstream workflow rejects it.

Evidence. HTTP 200, stop_reason: end_turn, the JSON parses, and a schema check fails on an enum. Replaying the recorded response through the validator fails the same way every time. So your code reads the response correctly; the response itself is off-contract.

Classification. Validation of model output.

Wrong instinct. Map refund_full to refund in a lenient post-processor. That silently invents business meaning.

Fix. Constrain generation, with structured outputs or a tool that has an enum in its input schema. With strict: true, the tool-use docs say inputs are guaranteed to match the schema. Keep a bounded repair for the semantic checks a schema can't express.
791f70074f:
Observed. The billing assistant tells some customers their balance is zero.

Evidence. The trace shows get_balance returning {"balance": 0} after 5,000 ms, which is the tool's timeout. The tool wrapper catches its own timeout and returns a default object.

Classification. A tool execution error disguised as a valid result, integration layer.

Fix. Never return a default for a failed read. Return a tool_result with is_error: true and a message such as "billing system timeout after 5 s; transient; do not state a balance". The tool-handling docs ask for exactly this kind of instructive message instead of a bare "failed". Section 08 covers the dispatcher design.
2006e56b33:
Observed. The outage assistant answers "no outage reported" for postcodes on the boundary of an outage polygon.

Evidence. Every integration check passes. The tool returns the right polygon, the result is in context, and stop_reason is end_turn. On 50 repeats of the same request, the answer is wrong 9 times.

Classification. Model output, statistical.

Fix. Not a prompt plea. Move the decision that code can make into code. Have the tool return {"in_outage": true}, computed geometrically, so the model reports a fact instead of inferring one from coordinates.

That's the general lesson of this class. When a model-output error is about a decision that's deterministic in principle, the best fix is often to make it deterministic in fact, by moving it into a tool.
da012aa61b:
Signature: stop_reason is max_tokens (or model_context_window_exceeded). Cause: your output cap is too low for this input, or the conversation filled the context window. Layer: integration, because the cap is your configuration.

Truncated JSON fails in json.loads, far from the cause. A lenient parser that "closes" open braces is worse: it turns the truncation into a silently incomplete object. The stop-reasons page adds a useful detail. If the truncation cuts through a tool_use block, retry with a higher max_tokens so the whole call arrives.
85a941dc85:
Signature: stop_reason: "refusal" in an HTTP 200, with stop_details identifying the policy category (the exact field shape is on the refusals page; check the docs). Cause: the safety classifiers declined this request on this model.

Fix: don't retry the identical request on the identical model in a loop. Restrictions differ between models, so the stop-reasons page recommends retrying on a fallback model. Otherwise, return a graceful message or route to a human. A spike in refusals after a prompt change can also signal that untrusted user content is being read as instructions (chapter 19).
660fc6b64b: Signature: end_turn with no content and a few output tokens. Cause: according to the stop-reasons page, it's usually text your code appended right after a tool_result in the same user turn. That teaches the model that the user speaks after tool results. Layer: integration. Fix the turn shape; don't resend the empty response. If it persists, the docs suggest a continuation prompt in a new user message.
86b06716e7:
Signature: your parser or validator rejects the text. It's not JSON, a key is missing, an enum value is outside the allowed set, or there's prose around the object. Layer: usually model output. But check the integration first. Was it truncated? Did your template drop the format instruction?

The strongest fix is to constrain generation. Structured outputs or a tool with an input schema guarantee the shape (chapter 18). They don't guarantee semantics: a schema-valid object can still carry the wrong order id. For what's left, a bounded repair prompt (section 11) works, because it gives the model the one thing it lacked: the precise error.
74c8a44066:
Signature: the model calls explain_bill for "my internet is down", or calls no tool when one was needed. You can't detect this from one response. You detect it with a labelled routing set (a list of inputs, each with the expected tool) run as an eval.

Cause: almost always overlapping or vague tool descriptions. Descriptions are the main signal the model uses to choose. Fix: rewrite each description with what the tool is for, example inputs and boundaries ("not for billing questions"). Split overloaded tools, and re-run the routing eval. Example 08 shows two of five routing cases failing with vague descriptions, and none with clear ones. Forcing a tool with tool_choice hides the symptom, and it's restricted on the newest models anyway (chapter 05).
9d5352e56b:
Signature: a fluent final answer that contradicts the data, often "you have no orders" after a lookup failed. Cause: frequently integration. The tool returned an empty list, or an error with no explanation, and the model drew the natural conclusion.

This is where reading the trace (section 14) matters most. The final message looks like a hallucination, but the root cause sits three turns earlier, in a tool result.
e78b515b7f:
Say a stem describes truncated JSON, an empty response after tool calls, or a crash while reading the response. The answer is an integration fix: check stop_reason, fix the turn shape, read blocks by type.

Now say it describes a consistent pattern of wrong choices, or format drift across many inputs. The answer is a model-facing fix (descriptions, examples, schema), verified by an eval. "Use a larger model" is rarely right for either.
cff98c8a82:
Refusal and truncation are the two model-output outcomes the API reports explicitly, through stop_reason. Both arrive as HTTP 200. That makes them the easiest model-output failures to detect, and also the most commonly mishandled. Generic error handling never sees them, and the partial content they carry looks usable.

This section goes one level below the summary in section 06. It covers what the response contains in each case, what the docs say to do, and the integration details where teams get it wrong: streaming, structured outputs, batches and server tools.
ae22b98e47: The word "refusal" covers three different mechanisms, and only one of them is a stop_reason. The streaming refusals page tells them apart. A debugging session that confuses them looks for evidence in the wrong place.
62f72a4281:
The first row is the one with an API contract. The refusals page documents its shape. stop_details carries type: "refusal", a category and an explanation. For every other stop reason it's null.

Both category and explanation can themselves be null, for example when the refusal maps to no named category. So the docs advise branching on stop_reason (or stop_details.type) and supplying your own user-facing message when the fields are empty. Code that does resp.stop_details["category"].upper() crashes on exactly the refusals it was written to handle.

You may show the explanation to the user, which is a reasonable default for a customer-facing assistant. The category belongs in your metrics.
9d4d87b776:
The third row is the trap in exam stems. A model that writes "I can't help with that" in plain text hasn't produced a refusal stop reason. No amount of stop_reason checking will count it.

If refusal-like answers rise after a prompt change, the detector is an evaluation over representative traffic, or a cheap classifier over final answers. The fix is usually in the prompt or the context. A common culprit is untrusted document text that reads like an instruction to the model.
9894b2df78:
In a stream, text deltas arrive before the stop reason. So a refusal decided part-way through generation arrives after some text is already on screen. The user may see "Sure, the first step is" followed by nothing.

The docs say stop_reason and stop_details arrive on the message_delta event. A streaming consumer has to treat every rendered delta as provisional until that event, and must be able to retract it. In a web UI, that means the message bubble stays pending until message_stop. On a refusal, it's replaced, not appended to.
1ace78e686:
The second rule is about history. The streaming refusals page says you must reset the conversation context after a refusal. Continuing without a reset leads to more refusals. It lists three ways to reset: remove the turn that triggered it, rephrase that turn, or clear the history.

For an agent loop, the practical consequence is simple. The refused assistant turn, partial text included, is never appended to messages. The broken pattern keeps the partial output and adds "please continue". That's the one that produces a run of refusals, and a support ticket saying "the model got stuck".

Example 25 shows both paths. The broken path keeps the partial turn and gets refused again, even on the second model. The fixed path discards the partial text, doesn't append the turn, and is served by the fallback.
421784099d:
The third rule is about where to retry. The stop-reasons page says a refused request on the current models can usually be served by retrying on another Claude model. It lists Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 among them. Re-sending the same request to the same model usually produces another refusal.

Three set-ups are documented: a server-side fallback configured on the API, SDK middleware, and a manual client-side retry. For the manual path, the docs describe a fallback credit that you pass on the retry, so you don't pay the prompt-cache cost twice. Check the docs for the exact parameter.

Haiku 5.5 is the exception. It has no server-side fallback, and its refusals carry no fallback credit, so a Haiku-first chain needs the retry in your own code. Whichever route you use, the response records which model served it. That belongs in the trace (section 13), for the same reason silent fallback does.
80f48cf3ee:
Two integration surfaces hide refusals.

Message Batches: the docs say batches report refusals as succeeded results with stop_reason: "refusal", not as errored results. A results processor that only counts errored and expired items, and resubmits those, will write refusals into the database as if they were answers. The fix is the same check as in the synchronous path, applied to every succeeded result.

Structured outputs: the structured-outputs page says that on a refusal the output may not match the schema, because the refusal takes precedence. So "we use structured outputs, so parsing can't fail" is false in two cases, refusal and truncation. The parser must look at stop_reason before it trusts the guarantee.
4407b6a9f4:
max_tokens means the response reached the cap you set. model_context_window_exceeded means the response filled the model's context window. That second one lets you ask for the maximum output without first computing the input size.

The stop-reasons page treats both as truncated output. It notes that the second value is currently typed only in the SDK's beta namespace (on newer models the API returns it without a beta header). What you do next depends on what was cut off, not on which of the two values you got.
3caffa4fb6:
The continuation pattern from the docs deserves a careful look, because it seems to clash with another rule. Claude 4.6+ models reject a prefilled final assistant message with a 400. The errors page lists it among common validation errors.

The continuation pattern isn't a prefill. The partial output goes in as an assistant message, but the request ends with a user message asking to continue. So the last turn is the user's.

Some code implemented continuation the older way: it sent the partial text as the final assistant turn and let the model extend it. That code breaks on upgrade, with exactly the 400 that case study C in section 17 starts from. Example 26 asserts that the last message of the continuation request has the user role.
cfbe16d776:
Two sizing rules prevent most truncation incidents.

First, size max_tokens for the largest legitimate output of the journey, not the average. Alert on the truncation rate (section 13), so you notice when inputs drift.

Second, keep long generations streamed. The errors page says the SDKs check that a non-streaming request isn't expected to exceed a 10-minute timeout, and it recommends streaming or batches for long requests. The stop-reasons example notes that the Python SDK requires streaming for max_tokens above roughly 21k. A team that raises max_tokens to fix truncation, then gets client-side errors on the same calls, has met this rule. client.messages.stream(...) with get_final_message() gives you the same Message back without per-event handling.
0b7b302335:
Agents that use server tools such as web search can receive stop_reason: "pause_turn". The docs say it's returned when the server-side sampling loop reaches its iteration limit (default 10 per request). The response may contain a server_tool_use block with no result yet. You continue by sending the assistant content back unchanged in a new request.

Treating it as a failure (logging an error and returning the partial content to the user) is an integration bug. It looks like the model "giving up half way". Treating it as unbounded is a cost bug; the documented helper caps continuations. Note that a response waiting on a client tool never has pause_turn. Its stop reason is tool_use.
945b936b9f:
The last line matters more than it looks. Stop reasons have been added over time: pause_turn, refusal and model_context_window_exceeded all arrived after the original three. A loop written as if tool_use ... else: finish treats every new value as a normal end.

An explicit dispatcher that raises on an unknown value turns the next addition into a failing test, instead of a silent behaviour change. The Java equivalent is a switch over the SDK's stop-reason type, with a default branch that throws.
6976bb1301:
When your tool throws, the loop can do one of three things.

  • It can crash. That kills a session the model could probably have recovered.
  • It can hide the error by returning an empty result. That tells the model "the data is empty" when the truth is "the data is unavailable", and it produces the confident wrong answer from section 06.
  • It can report the error as data: a tool_result for that tool_use_id with is_error: true and a message the model can act on.

Only the third keeps the protocol valid (every tool_use must be answered) and keeps the model informed.
85666f9b76:
"Actionable" is the key word. The model can only choose a sensible next step if the message says what kind of failure it was. So draw three distinctions:

  • transient versus permanent ("billing DB timed out, retrying may work" vs "account A-404 does not exist");
  • access failure versus a valid empty result ("no orders found for C-7" is not an error);
  • argument errors versus system errors ("date must be YYYY-MM-DD, got 03/04").

For an unknown tool name, list the available tools. Keep stack traces and internal hostnames out of the message. It goes into the context window, and the model may repeat it to the user.
966b3b7938:
Two policies belong in the dispatcher, not the model.

Retries of idempotent reads (one quick retry on a timeout) are cheaper in code than in a model turn.

Side-effecting tools (refunds, cancellations, port-outs) must not be retried blindly by either party. If the first call timed out after the downstream system committed, a retry double-refunds. Give such tools an idempotency key derived from the conversation and the action, exactly as you would for a payment API. On a duplicate, the tool reports "already applied".
49d1c11dba: A tool failure passes through four hands before anyone sees it: the tool, the dispatcher, the model and, in a multi-agent system, a coordinator. Each hand can preserve the information or destroy it. The failures in section 14's trace and in case study B (section 17) are both cases where an early hand destroyed it. It helps to name what each hand is responsible for.
80d0a8522e:
The tool knows the most: the downstream status, the exception type, whether the operation committed. Its job is to raise a specific exception, not to decide what the conversation should do. A tool that catches its own failure and returns a default ([], 0, None) has already made the worst decision available. Every later hand now sees success.

The dispatcher is the translation layer between your exceptions and the protocol. It owns three decisions that are code, not judgement:

  • the classification of the exception (transient, permanent, bad arguments, permission, not found);
  • the cheap local recovery (one retry of an idempotent read);
  • the limits (how many times the same call may fail in one run).

It writes the result as a tool_result with is_error: true and a message written for the model.
35a2a538fd:
The model owns the recovery that needs language: asking the user for a missing identifier, choosing a different tool, explaining that a system is unavailable. The tool-handling docs describe this division directly. With is_error set, Claude works the error into its response. When a call is invalid or missing parameters, it retries two or three times with corrections before apologising to the user.

That retry behaviour helps with argument errors and wastes turns on permanent system errors. That's why the message must say which one it is. The docs also give the prevention for the argument case: strict: true on a tool definition guarantees that inputs match the schema. Missing parameters and type mismatches stop happening at all.

The coordinator, when there is one, receives a subagent's result as text or structured data. A subagent that summarises "I found no orders" after three failed lookups has done to the coordinator what a swallowing tool does to the model. Subagent results need the same structure: status, what was attempted, partial results, and whether retrying could help.
c038be2c80:
The structure can be JSON inside the content string, as in example 23. The protocol only requires a string or content blocks, so the shape is your choice. Keep it consistent across tools, though, so a guard can parse it.

In MCP servers, the same idea is the isError flag on a tool result. The MCP spec separates protocol-level errors from tool execution errors. Protocol errors (an unknown tool, malformed arguments) are reported as JSON-RPC errors. Execution errors are reported inside a successful result with isError: true, so the model can see them. An MCP client that turns a protocol error into an exception, and an isError result into a tool_result with is_error, preserves the distinction end to end (chapter 22; check the MCP spec for the exact result shape of your protocol version).
d9df92cf52:
The model decides how to recover. Your code decides how much recovery a run may spend. Three guards cover nearly every runaway loop.

Identical-failure guard: count failures per (tool, canonical input) within a run. On the third identical failure, stop executing that call: return a terminal message, or end the run with a handoff. Example 23 shows a model that ignores retryable: false being stopped this way on the third call.

Per-run tool-error budget: across all tools, more than N errors in one run means something systemic is wrong. End the run and escalate, rather than letting the model try every tool in turn.

Turn and token caps: set a hard maximum number of turns, and of input tokens, per run. Record hitting it as a distinct outcome (stopped: max_turns), so it shows up in metrics as a failure and not a normal end.

Caps are a safety net. They're not the primary stop mechanism; that's still the model ending its turn. An exam stem that offers "raise the iteration cap" as the fix for a loop is offering to pay more for the same failure.
2f1e62f692:
Every recovery strategy has a precondition.

  • Retrying assumes the failure is transient and the call is safe to repeat.
  • A fallback model assumes another model can do the job, and that the failure is specific to the first one.
  • A repair prompt assumes the model can fix the output once told what's wrong.
  • A circuit breaker assumes the dependency is unhealthy for everyone, not just for this request.

Apply a strategy whose precondition is false and it doesn't merely fail. It adds load, cost or latency on top of the original failure.
bd6b159904: The SDKs already retry connection errors, 408, 409, 429 and 5xx twice by default, with exponential backoff, and they honour retry-after (chapter 05 has the details). That leaves you two decisions: where the retry policy lives, and what happens when the SDK's attempts run out.
25497a1278: One layer owns retries. Say the SDK retries twice, your service wrapper retries three times, and the API gateway in front retries twice more. During an overload, one user request can then become 3 × 4 × 3 = 36 calls, and an overload is exactly when the extra load hurts. Pick one layer and make every other layer pass failures through. Usually that's the SDK with a tuned max_retries, or your own wrapper with the SDK set to max_retries=0.
f232b18680:
Jitter is what makes backoff work under load. Example 02 simulates 200 clients that all receive a 529 at the same moment. With plain exponential backoff, all 200 retry at exactly 1s, then 3s, then 7s. The service sees four synchronised spikes of 200 requests each.

With full jitter (a uniform random delay between zero and the exponential ceiling), the busiest 250 ms window drops to about 70 requests. The retries spread across roughly 50 windows. The total work is the same. The peak, which is what overloads the service, is about a third.
a29a0f908e: In Java, the same policy is a few lines of Resilience4j configuration, and it composes with the breaker in section 12. If Resilience4j owns the policy, set the Anthropic Java client's own retries to zero. The client builder has a maxRetries option; check the Java SDK docs for the exception class names to match on.
aff8c5287b:
The "one layer owns retries" rule deserves its arithmetic. Attempts multiply across layers. So the worst-case number of calls per user request is the product of each layer's attempt count, not the sum.

Example 19 computes 3 × 4 × 3 = 36: a gateway with three attempts, a service wrapper with four, and the SDK's default of three (one try plus two retries). In normal operation the multiplier is invisible, because the first attempt succeeds. In an overload, every layer exhausts its budget. The dependency then receives up to 36 times the user traffic, at the moment it can least absorb it.

That's how a short capacity event turns into a long one. The retries keep the service overloaded after the original burst is over.
f390e133f3:
Even a single retry layer can amplify too much when every request fails. A retry budget bounds retries as a fraction of first attempts over a sliding window. For example, retries may be at most 10% of requests, with a small floor so a quiet service can still retry a lone failure.

Under normal conditions the budget is never reached. During an outage, it caps the extra load at 10% instead of 300%. Example 19 simulates 1,000 users during a total outage. Four attempts each produce 4,000 calls; the budgeted policy produces about 1,100.

The idea comes from RPC frameworks. Finagle and gRPC both have retry throttling (check their docs for the exact algorithms). It's worth borrowing for any shared Claude gateway.
86c3715aec:
Three companion rules complete the policy.

Deadlines, not attempt counts, protect users. An interactive request has a latency budget. A retry that can't finish inside it is wasted work, which is why the wrapper in this section checks elapsed time before sleeping.

Timeouts must be set deliberately. The SDK default timeout is long, because generations can be long. For a short classification call, a tighter per-request timeout plus one retry gives better tail latency than one long wait (chapter 05 has the client options; check the docs for current defaults).

Only idempotent work is retried automatically. A Messages API call has no side effects, so it's always safe to repeat. The agent step that wraps it may not be. If a retry re-runs a tool loop that already called create_ticket, you open two tickets. Retry the model call, not the step, or make the step idempotent.
4464b18a5c: In a Spring Boot service, the policy usually lives in configuration rather than code, through the Resilience4j Spring Boot starter. The instance names are yours. The property names below follow the Resilience4j documentation, but check it for your version.
ed24273282:
A Python service has three reasonable owners for retry policy, and your choice decides which knobs exist.

The SDK alone: keep the default retries (two retries, exponential backoff, retry-after honoured, per the errors page). Tune them with the client's max_retries and timeout options, or per call with client.with_options(max_retries=..., timeout=...). This is the right default for interactive calls. The SDK already classifies connection errors, 408, 409, 429 and 5xx as retryable, and leaves 4xx alone. What it doesn't know is your deadline, your spend-cap rule (a 429 without retry-after) or your fallback chain.

A retry library such as tenacity, with the SDK set to max_retries=0, gives you a predicate, a stop condition and a wait strategy as composable pieces. The tenacity names below are its documented API, but check its docs for your version.

Your own wrapper is about forty lines (example 29). You write it when the policy needs data the library doesn't have, such as a shared retry budget across workers (example 19).
2b130fed27:
Two details in that snippet are easy to get wrong.

reraise=True makes the decorator raise the last real exception instead of the library's own wrapper error. That way the fallback layer outside can still tell a 529 from a 400. And the stop condition combines attempts with elapsed time. That's the deadline rule from earlier in this section, in library form.

One thing the snippet doesn't do is honour retry-after exactly; wait_random_exponential ignores headers. If capacity 429s are common in your traffic, you have two options. Let the SDK own retries, since it honours the header. Or write a custom wait function that reads it, as example 29 does: when the header is present, its value wins over the computed delay.
e0f785f61d: Full jitter is the default recommendation, but it's one of several. At exam level, the only point is that you need some randomisation. The variants trade spread against waiting time in different ways. Example 29 runs 200 clients through three retry rounds with each strategy and counts the busiest 250 ms window.
0d12004573:
The numbers are specific to the simulation (three rounds, a 1 s base, a 30 s cap). Don't read them as a general ranking. What generalises is the shape. Any jitter removes the synchronised spike. Choosing between variants is a second-order tuning decision. The precondition questions matter far more: is this failure retryable, who owns the retry, and what's the deadline?

In Resilience4j, IntervalFunction.ofExponentialRandomBackoff is the randomised exponential policy shown earlier. Its randomisation factor of 0.5 means each delay is drawn from 50% to 150% of the exponential value. That's closer to equal jitter than to full jitter.
eed92c0b1c:
A fallback chain (for example claude-opus-5-5, then claude-sonnet-5-5, then claude-haiku-5-5) answers two failures. One is sustained overload of one model. The other is refusals, which the docs say another model can often serve.

It must not answer request errors. Falling back on a 400 sends the same malformed request to a second model and hides the bug in your dashboards. It also shouldn't be silent. A cheaper model may be fine for a summary and wrong for a contract clause. So the decision belongs to the product owner, per task, and every response should record which model actually produced it (example 04, and the trace fields in section 13).

Before relying on a fallback, run your eval set against it. A fallback nobody has measured is a guess.
4b90d145c6:
Model fallback is one form of graceful degradation. Other forms are often better for a given product:

  • serve a cached answer for a common question;
  • return a deterministic template ("your bill is available in the app");
  • queue the request and notify the user later;
  • hand off to a human agent, with the context collected so far.

Decide these per user journey, in advance. An incident is a bad time to design them.
d20df2c5e8:
Silent fallback is the failure mode of a working fallback. Example 18 runs 20 contract-summary requests during a partial overload. The fallback model serves 7 of them, and every response is HTTP 200. From the transport's point of view nothing is broken. Meanwhile the product quietly ships a third of its summaries from a model nobody evaluated for that journey.

The protection is two fields and one alert. Record model_requested and model_served on every response (the response's model field tells you what actually ran). Compute a fallback rate per journey. Alert when it exceeds what the product owner accepted. For a quality-critical journey the accepted rate may be zero. Then the right degradation is a queue or a human, not a cheaper model.
7c936878db: In Java, Resilience4j's Decorators builder composes the pieces and adds the fallback as the outermost step. The fallback function receives the exception, so it can refuse to degrade on the wrong class.
a774e1efa2:
A repair prompt sends the invalid output back with the validator's exact complaint and asks for a corrected version. It works when the information exists and the model made a formatting or constraint mistake. It fails, at full cost, when the input simply doesn't contain the value. Ask three times for an order id that isn't in the ticket, and you get three guesses.

Three rules make it safe:

  • The validator is deterministic code, not another model call.
  • The message names the precise problem ('action' must be one of ['credit', 'none', 'refund'], got 'refund_full'). "Fix your JSON" gives the model nothing to work with.
  • The number of repairs is bounded, usually one or two. After that, the item goes to a dead-letter queue or a human.
74e3a466f8: Prefer prevention to repair. With structured outputs or a tool input schema, shape errors disappear. The repair loop then only handles semantic checks, such as an amount that doesn't match the invoice or a date in the future. If repairs are frequent, the prompt or schema is wrong. Count them as a metric rather than treating them as normal.
e7d31f6fa0:
Retries help one request survive a short blip. During a real outage they make things worse. Every request spends its full retry budget. Threads and connections pile up waiting on backoff sleeps, and the caller's latency and memory degrade along with the dependency.

A circuit breaker watches the failure rate. Once the rate crosses a threshold, the breaker opens: calls fail immediately for a cool-down period, so the caller can serve its fallback at once. After the cool-down, the breaker goes half-open and lets a probe through. Success closes it; failure re-opens it.
d35c777915:
Two details are specific to Claude integrations.

Only health failures should count: 5xx, 529, connection errors and capacity 429s. A 400 means your request is wrong. It says nothing about the dependency's health, and it shouldn't open a breaker that then blocks valid requests (example 03 asserts this).

And scope the breaker sensibly. Per model is usually right, since one model can be overloaded while another is fine. That lets the breaker drive the fallback chain from section 11.
b00f4eabb5: The order of decoration matters: breaker outside, retry inside. That way an open breaker short-circuits before any retry sleeps, and a whole retried call counts as one outcome in the breaker's window. Example 03 is the same state machine in about thirty lines of Python, with an injectable clock. That's how you test it.
ed355ff839:
Example 21 assembles the full stack in Python and asserts the property that justifies the order. Opus returns 529 on every call. The first two user requests each spend three attempts and two backoff sleeps inside the retry, and each counts as one failed outcome in the breaker. The breaker then opens. The next requests go straight to Sonnet: zero Opus calls, zero sleeps.

Reverse the order (retry outside the breaker) and an open breaker would raise CallNotPermittedException into the retry. The retry would sleep and try again three times per request, adding latency for no possible benefit.
8fec56017a:
Two more Resilience4j modules matter for Claude calls.

A time limiter enforces the user-facing deadline independently of the SDK's transport timeout. A slow generation is abandoned once the user has stopped waiting.

A bulkhead caps concurrent in-flight Claude calls per journey. A surge of long agent runs then can't take every connection and starve the short billing lookups. In a servlet stack, this is the same thread-pool isolation you already apply to slow downstream systems. The bulkhead is also the cheapest defence against your own rate limit. If the tier allows a known number of concurrent requests' worth of tokens per minute, admitting more only turns them into 429s.
a14b2e8a3e:
The simplest breaker opens after N consecutive failures. It's easy to write and easy to test. It's also the wrong design for a dependency with a non-zero background failure rate.

Suppose 30% of calls fail during a degraded period that the product can tolerate. Three failures in a row then happen by chance about 2.7% of the time on any given call. Over two thousand calls, the consecutive breaker opens dozens of times. Example 28 measures it: 41 openings, each one sending a burst of healthy-enough traffic to the fallback or the error page.

Resilience4j uses a different design: a failure-rate breaker over a sliding window, with a minimum number of calls before it may decide. With a 50% threshold over a 50-call window and a 20-call minimum, it opened twice in the same run. Both designs open quickly in a real outage: the consecutive breaker after 3 calls, the rate breaker after 20, the minimum.
051a8d610f:
That last number is the trade-off you're choosing. The minimum-calls setting is the price of statistical stability. Below it the breaker refuses to judge, so during a sudden total outage it lets minimum requests fail before opening.

For a high-traffic journey, 20 calls is a fraction of a second. For a journey with two calls a minute, it's ten minutes of failures, and a time-based window or a lower minimum fits better. Resilience4j exposes these choices directly: slidingWindowType (COUNT_BASED or TIME_BASED), slidingWindowSize, minimumNumberOfCalls, failureRateThreshold, waitDurationInOpenState and permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState.
f501d241cc:
Resilience4j can also open on slow calls (slowCallRateThreshold with slowCallDurationThreshold). This setting needs care with a language model. A generation's latency is roughly proportional to the number of output tokens, so a long, correct answer is slow by design. A slow-call threshold tuned on short classification calls will open the breaker when a user asks for a detailed explanation.

There are two ways out. Scope slow-call breakers per journey, with thresholds measured on that journey's distribution. Or measure time to first token on streamed calls, which reflects queueing and overload rather than answer length. The same reasoning applies to the time limiter: the user-facing deadline is per journey.
d3603d2c7c:
Python has no single dominant breaker library. Small libraries exist (pybreaker is one; check its docs for its configuration names). Many teams write the forty lines themselves, as examples 03 and 28 do. The two Claude-specific rules, count only health failures and scope per model, are easier to see in code you own.

Whatever the implementation, emit the state transitions as events and metrics. A breaker that opens without anyone noticing is a silent fallback with extra steps. Resilience4j publishes state-transition events for exactly this purpose, and Micrometer binds them to metrics.
939851511d:
An agent run is a sequence of model turns and tool calls. When it fails, you need to reconstruct what the model saw at each turn, what it decided, and what came back, without access to the user's session. That decides what to record.

The rule is the one Dapper established. Use one trace id for the whole run and one record (span) per unit of work. Put enough attributes on each record to answer questions you haven't thought of yet.
1ced04706e:
Two constraints shape the design.

Size: if you store every full request for a 30-turn agent, you store the growing transcript 30 times. Log hashes and previews per turn instead. Keep full request and response bodies in a separate store with a short retention, sampled or kept for failed runs. That's also what replay (section 16) needs.

Privacy: transcripts contain customer data. Redact or tokenise PII before it leaves the process. Restrict access to the full-body store, and apply the same retention rules as any other customer record (chapter 19). For a telecom support agent, that means phone numbers and account ids are hashed in logs. The mapping is available only to whoever is cleared to see it.
cf10f085e9:
Per-turn records answer "what happened in this run". Operations also needs to know "is the service healthy right now". That's a handful of rates computed from the same records.

The key design point: most of these rates are computed over successful HTTP responses, because the failures they measure arrive as 200s. A dashboard that only shows HTTP error rate and latency stays green while users receive truncated answers, refusals, and answers built on failed tools. Example 20 computes the rates below from a small sample. Of the four alerts it triggers, only one is visible to an HTTP-only dashboard.
02c5a77bb0:
On the JVM, these are Micrometer counters and timers tagged by journey, model, stop_reason and error class, scraped like any other service metric.

OpenTelemetry's generative-AI semantic conventions define span attribute names for the model requested and served, token usage and finish reasons. Use them and an off-the-shelf backend can draw the panels without custom parsing. The conventions are still marked as in development, though, so pin the version you emit and check the OpenTelemetry docs for current names.

Cardinality deserves the usual care. Tag by journey and model, never by customer id or prompt hash.
c2b02e40c6:
You read a failed agent trace the way you read any distributed trace. Start from the symptom, walk backwards to the first record that's wrong, and classify that record. The symptom is almost never the cause.

Here's the recorded trace from the companion (trace_bad.jsonl). A support agent was asked "where is my order?" and answered "You have no orders on file", to a customer who has an order.
6652ab7b85:
Walk backwards. Turn 5 is a wrong answer, but given turns 2 to 4 it's a reasonable reading of three empty results. Turns 3 and 4 are a loop, but the model is retrying because it was told only "error" and nothing else. Turn 2's tool result is the first wrong record: the tool flagged an error and gave no message.

A model can't tell "the order service is down" from "the customer has no orders" when both come back as []. So the defect is in the integration layer, in the tool's error reporting. The fixes, in order:

  1. Make get_orders return an actionable message ("order service timeout; transient").
  2. Have the dispatcher retry the read once itself.
  3. Add a rule or hook so an answer asserting absence of data can't follow a failed lookup.
  4. Add this trace as a regression case.
dc8a2cd9d4:
Example 10 encodes the checks that point at this answer automatically. They generalise to most traces:

  • repeated identical tool calls (a loop: the model isn't getting what it needs);
  • error results with empty bodies (opaque errors);
  • final answers asserting absence after tool errors (masked failure);
  • monotonic input-token growth (context bloat, which matters for long runs and cost; chapter 16).

A few other signatures are worth scanning for. A tool_use whose arguments contain values that appear nowhere earlier in the transcript means fabricated arguments, a model-output error. A change of system_hash or model mid-run means a deploy or fallback during the session. And watch for stop_reason values other than tool_use or end_turn in the middle of a run.
d871d4a1dd:
Walking backwards from the symptom works when the trace is short. A 30-turn agent run with parallel tool calls is a different matter. Reading it end to end is slow and error-prone.

A fixed sequence of narrow passes is faster. Each pass reads one or two fields across every record and asks one question. The first three passes settle most incidents, and they read only fields that the per-turn record in section 13 already contains.
84433c6132:
The passes are ordered by cost and by yield.

  • Pass 1 needs one field per model turn. It catches the whole family of "loop did not handle a stop reason" defects.
  • Pass 2 finds the first failure, which is usually near the root cause.
  • Pass 3 is a grouping query.
  • Pass 4 is the only one that needs content. It separates "the model invented an id" from "the code passed the wrong id".
  • Passes 5 and 6 explain cost incidents and "it changed on Tuesday" incidents, respectively.

Example 10 automates passes 2, 3 and 5. Adding pass 1 is a lab exercise.
31ad7d4f26:
Pass 1: ten tool_use turns and no end_turn. The run ended on the cap, and the run record says so explicitly. An outcome field such as stopped:max_turns is worth adding precisely so this pass is one query.

Pass 2: the first tool record is already an error, five characters long, with the body error.

Pass 3: ten identical get_orders calls.

Three passes and a few seconds of reading. The investigation has moved from "the model is looping" to "why does get_orders fail, and why doesn't the model know what kind of failure it is?" The latency of 40 ms is a clue too. A timeout would take seconds, so this is a fast rejection. That points at a contract or permission problem rather than an overloaded service.
04c21f8a3f: One walkthrough teaches the method. But the exam, and real incidents, reward recognising several trace shapes on sight. The two runs below fail in ways that look like model problems from the outside, and aren't. Read each trace table before the analysis, and try to name the first wrong record yourself.
d4116be680: Report. A network-operations agent receives an outage report for six cell sites and is told to open one P1 incident. The ticket appears in the ticketing system with priority normal and only two sites. The on-call engineer's first message in the incident channel is "the model ignored the instructions". Here's the trace (example 16 reproduces it):
d0fa7d705a:
Step 1, start at the symptom. The symptom is a tool side effect, so the first record to read is the tool call that produced it. The input really did contain two sites and no priority. The model's later message is irrelevant; the damage was done by then.

Step 2, ask why the call looked like that. The model turn that emitted it has stop_reason: max_tokens. A tool_use block from a turn that hit the output cap was cut off while it was being generated. The arguments the model intended (six sites, P1) never arrived. The stop-reasons page says to retry with a higher max_tokens when truncation cuts through a tool call. That's the documented reading of this exact record.

Step 3, find the first wrong record. It's turn 1 of the model. The defect isn't that the model stopped. It's that the loop executed a tool call from a truncated turn.

Step 4, classify. Integration layer, twice over. The cap of 64 tokens is configuration, and the loop's missing check is code.

Step 5, fix.

  • Never execute tools when stop_reason is not tool_use.
  • On max_tokens, re-request with a larger cap (example 16 doubles it and gets the full call).
  • Size max_tokens for the largest legitimate tool input, not the average.
  • For side-effecting tools, validate required fields in the tool itself. A P1 ticket without a priority should be rejected with an instructive is_error, not defaulted.
05db728480: The general signature is a side effect that matches a prefix of the intended action. Whenever a downstream record is a truncated version of what was asked for, read the stop_reason of the turn that produced the call before you read anything else.
a34af543f0: Report. A customer-care assistant has check_outage and get_bill. Questions that need one tool work. Questions such as "my internet is down, is my bill affected?" fail on the second API call with HTTP 400. A ticket to the platform team says "the API rejects parallel tool use". Here's the trace (example 17):
0d4cecb75e:
Step 1, the symptom is a 4xx. That alone settles the layer. A 400 says the request is malformed, so the defect is in what your code built. The model's behaviour (calling two tools in one turn, which is normal) isn't in question.

Step 2, read the error message literally. The tool-handling docs list this exact message. They say tool results must immediately follow the assistant turn that requested them, with tool_result blocks first in the content array.

Step 3, compare the rendered messages with the rule. The assistant turn requested two tools. The message immediately after it answers only toolu_01. The result for toolu_02 arrives one message later, which isn't "immediately after". Two consecutive user messages are also a shape smell on their own; example 13's invariant checker flags them before the call.

Step 4, fix. The dispatcher collects all results for one assistant turn into a single user message, results first, any text after.

Step 5, guard. Run the request invariants before each call, in development and in CI on recorded traces. The next shape bug then fails with your message, not the API's.
5bffa2e597:
The lesson for reading traces: a 4xx in the middle of an agent run points at the previous append, not the previous response. The model's last response was fine. The code that turned it into history was not.

This is also the most common way a refactor of an agent loop breaks production. The happy path with one tool keeps working. The shape bug only shows on the turns where the model uses tools in parallel.
ae11233053: When the trace doesn't settle it, isolate. Each step below removes one layer from the question. The order puts the cheap, deterministic steps first.
9d73023ce4:
If you record request and response bodies (section 13), you can replace the client with a replayer. It returns the recorded response for an identical request. Replay removes the model completely. If the failure reproduces on replay, it's in your code, every time. You can fix it with a debugger and pin it with a test that uses the same recording.

Example 11 records a response whose first block is a thinking block. The code under test reads content[0].text and fails on 5 of 5 replays, and the fix is verified against the same recording. A replayer that raises on an unknown request is useful too. It tells you the code now sends something different from what was recorded, and that's a lead in itself.
1c37d2c3a8:
A scripted fake that returns a correct response exercises the whole path (request building, dispatch, tool handling, parsing, rendering) with the model's variability removed. If the pipeline fails with a known-good response, the integration is broken.

In Java, this is a hand-written fake of a small ClaudeGateway interface, or WireMock stubbing /v1/messages with recorded bodies and 429/529 responses. You already do this for every other dependency, and that's the point.
ef0b67ca41:
If the integration passes with good output, look at what the model was actually sent. Not the template in the repository, but the rendered request, after variables, retrieval results and conversation history were filled in. "It got worse after Tuesday's deploy" is usually answered by diffing a rendered request from Monday against one from Wednesday.

Example 12 shows a refactor that renamed a customer field. A .get() hid the KeyError, and the system prompt now says Customer tier: None. So the model stopped offering retention credits. Nothing about the model changed. A deterministic guard that rejects rendered prompts containing None, unreplaced braces or empty sections would have caught it before deploy.
d2b23b777a:
Diff the other inputs too:

  • the model id actually returned (an alias that moved to a new snapshot changes behaviour with no code change);
  • the tool definitions;
  • the retrieval results;
  • the length of the history (a bug that drops older turns looks like the model forgetting).
3dae0b2be4:
Many integration bugs are visible in the request without calling anything: the first message isn't from the user, two user turns in a row, a tool_use without a matching tool_result, text before the tool results, empty content, max_tokens above the model's limit. Example 13 runs these as assertions.

In production they run before each call, so you fail fast with a clear message instead of a 400 from the API. In CI they run on recorded traces. The same applies to responses. Truncation, refusal, empty end_turn and "expected JSON" checks are code, not judgement.
3cda33e594:
Only when steps 1 to 4 pass is it a model-output problem. And then a single rerun proves nothing. Send the same rendered request N times and count failures.

The arithmetic matters. If the true failure rate is 5%, twenty runs show at least one failure only 1 − 0.9520 ≈ 64% of the time. So "I ran it 20 times and it was fine" is weak evidence. To be 95% sure of seeing a 5% failure at least once, you need about 59 runs (0.9559 ≈ 0.05). To claim a fix cut the rate from 5% to 2%, you need a few hundred runs per variant.

For a rare failure, reproduce it on the cases that triggered it in production, rather than on random inputs.
1187a75ab6: A common distractor proposes setting temperature: 0 to make the model deterministic for debugging. On the newest models, non-default sampling parameters are rejected (chapter 05). Even where they're accepted, low temperature reduces variation without guaranteeing identical outputs. Determinism for debugging comes from replay and fakes, which remove the model, not from sampling settings.
e1fd8e65c2: Written as a runbook, each step has an input you need, an observation, and a conclusion you're allowed to draw from it. The conclusions are deliberately narrow. A step that passes doesn't prove the other layer guilty. It only removes its own layer from suspicion.
485a5b7a92: Time-box it. Once recording is in place, steps 1 to 4 take minutes. They settle most production incidents, because most production incidents are integration incidents. If you find yourself on step 5 without having done step 3, stop. A rendered-request diff costs nothing, and step 5 costs N calls.
89662bc189:
A team migrated its contract-extraction service from one model snapshot to claude-sonnet-5-5. In the same release, it changed its HTTP client library. Afterwards, 4% of extractions fail validation. The model change is the obvious suspect, which is exactly why the procedure runs first.

Step 1: the failing responses were recorded. Replayed through the current parser, 31 of 40 parse correctly. So the parser is rejecting valid responses, and the remaining 9 are genuinely invalid. That's two problems, not one.

The 31: the diff between old and new parsing code shows the cause. When a proxy's rewritten header drops the charset, the new HTTP library decodes the body as Latin-1. That mangles accented company names into invalid JSON escape sequences. Integration, deterministic, fixed with an explicit UTF-8 decode and a replay test.

The 9: steps 2 to 4 pass, and the rendered request is unchanged apart from the model id. Repeating the 9 inputs 20 times each gives 41 failures out of 180, all on contracts with two signatories where the schema allows one. That's a model-output problem with a real rate: about 23% on that input class, about 1% overall. The fix was to change the schema to an array of signatories and add those contracts to the eval set.

Without step 1, the team would have spent the week on prompts and blamed the model for a character-encoding bug.
1c3fdd43a1:
Step 1 of the procedure depends on a replay harness, and the replayer shown above is the bare minimum. A harness a team will actually use for months needs answers to five design questions.

The pattern is old. Ruby's VCR and Python's VCR.py call the recordings "cassettes", and WireMock has record and playback on the JVM. What's specific to Claude is what goes into the key, and what has to be stored verbatim.
5af8716193:
1. What is the key? The key is a hash of the parts of the request that can change the model's behaviour: model, system, messages, tools, tool_choice, max_tokens, thinking and effort settings, output_config, stop_sequences.

Remove fields that can't change behaviour before hashing: metadata, stream, timeouts and client headers. Otherwise every replay misses because a user id or a timeout changed. The JSON must also be canonical (sorted keys, fixed separators), so two equal requests hash the same. Example 27 changes metadata.user_id between recording and replay and still gets a hit. Then it adds a system prompt and gets a miss.
73c4241de3:
2. What is stored? The full response content blocks, verbatim, plus stop_reason, stop_details, usage and the model that served it.

Verbatim matters most for thinking blocks. The errors page says that edited, reordered, filtered or reconstructed thinking blocks in the latest assistant message are rejected with a 400. A harness that stores only text and rebuilds the blocks later produces requests the live API refuses. Store the blocks exactly as the API returned them.
2bf24c4c4d:
3. What happens on a miss? Three modes cover the needs.

  • Record calls through and saves.
  • Replay never calls the model and raises on a miss. That's what CI and debugging need. A miss is itself evidence that the code now sends something different, and the diff between the recorded request and the new one is often the bug. (A miss after a refactor is how the Customer tier: None regression in example 12 would surface.)
  • New episodes replays known requests and records unknown ones. It suits extending a suite.

Never fall back silently from replay to live in a test. A test that sometimes calls the model is a flaky test with a bill.
2bc8d3e132:
4. What about tools? An agent run interleaves model turns and tool calls. If the tools are live during replay, a tool that returns different data today changes the next request. The key changes, and replay misses from turn 2 onwards.

So record tool results in the same cassette, keyed by tool name and canonical input, and replay them too. Then a whole multi-turn run replays deterministically. A change in your loop code (how it appends results, which stop reasons it handles) gets tested against exactly the responses that exposed the bug.
6a8d1caf0f:
5. Where does PII go? Cassettes are transcripts. Redact before the key is computed and before anything is written. Then the stored file never holds a phone number, and the key stays stable across customers with the same request shape. Example 27 checks that the recorded file contains <PHONE> and not the number.

Keep cassettes for real incidents in the same restricted store as full request bodies (section 13). Commit only synthetic or fully redacted ones to the repository.
ef66a856fe:
On the JVM, the same harness is usually WireMock in front of the Anthropic Java client. Point the client's base URL at WireMock (the Java client builder has a base-URL option; check the Java SDK docs for its name). Record against the real API once, then run the suite in playback, with request matching on the JSON body. WireMock's equalToJson matcher can ignore fields, which covers the volatile-field rule from question 1.

You can point the Python SDK at a local stub the same way, through its base_url option. That's useful when the system under test isn't your Python code but a service you can only configure.
df33ff4700:
Replay has one limit worth stating plainly. It proves what your code does with a given response. It can't tell you whether the model would still produce that response.

After a model upgrade, recorded responses from the old model are still valid tests of your parser and loop. But they say nothing about the new model's output. That question belongs to step 5 and to the eval set, run in shadow against the new model before the switch. That's exactly what would have caught case study C in section 17.
03439d8d99:
The walkthroughs in sections 14 and 15 start from a single trace. Real incidents start earlier, with a vague report. Getting from the report to the trace is half the job.

Each case below follows the same five stages:

  • the symptoms as they were reported;
  • the trace evidence collected before any change;
  • the isolation step that settled the layer;
  • the root cause;
  • the fix, with the test or metric that now guards it.

All three cases are runnable in the companion (examples 22, 23 and 24), and the numbers come from those runs.
828b70123f:
Symptoms. A telecom operator runs a nightly job at 02:00. It summarises the previous day's 400 escalated support tickets for the morning shift. Most nights it completes. On some nights, though, 60 to 110 summaries are missing, the job log shows overloaded_error, and the morning report goes out incomplete.

The operations team's ticket says "Claude API unreliable at night; consider another provider". Nothing in the code changed between good and bad nights.
caea551883:
Trace evidence. Before touching anything, collect three facts from the per-attempt records.

First, every failure is HTTP 529 overloaded_error. The errors page describes this as the API being temporarily overloaded, which can happen when there's high traffic across all users. It is not a 429 tied to this organisation's limits.

Second, the failed items' attempt timestamps are 02:00:00, 02:00:02 and 02:00:04. That's three attempts inside four seconds.

Third, failures don't correlate with ticket length, language or content. They correlate only with start time. On good nights there are no 529s at all in the job's window.
d461c3a0e9:
Isolation step. Two cheap checks settle the layer.

First, replay the failed items at 10:00 with the same code. All of them succeed. So the requests are valid and the content is irrelevant. This is not a model-output problem, and not a request bug.

Then do the arithmetic. Say a platform-wide overload window answers 529 to about 60% of requests for a few seconds. A request that makes three attempts inside that window fails all three with probability 0.63 ≈ 22%. That predicts about 86 failures out of 400; the observed count was 60 to 110. The job's retry policy, not the API, decides whether a short overload window becomes lost work. Example 22 simulates exactly this: the naive job loses 95 of 400 items and makes 817 calls.
b3777d5b02:
Root cause. Integration layer, job design. Three choices combine:

  • All 400 requests start in the same second. There's no ramp, which also invites the acceleration-limit 429s that the errors page warns about for sudden usage spikes.
  • The wrapper retries on a fixed two-second sleep, so the whole retry budget is spent inside a window a few seconds long.
  • Failed items are dropped instead of being resubmitted.

The API's overload was real but short. A batch job with an hour of slack has no reason to give up after four seconds.
4152a9d132:
Fix. Ramp admission (35 requests per second in the simulation). Back off with full jitter, capped at 30 seconds. After the main pass, resubmit only the failed item ids a minute later. Example 22's fixed run loses 6 items in the first pass and none after the resubmission.

The longer-term fix is to ask whether the job needs the synchronous API at all. A nightly summary is the textbook Message Batches workload (chapter 07). The batch is processed asynchronously, and you resubmit only the errored results by custom_id. Remember the batch-specific check from section 07: refusals come back as succeeded results, so the results processor must read stop_reason as well.

Guard: a metric of items failed per run, an alert when it's above zero, and the attempt timestamps in the per-attempt record. The next investigation then starts at the evidence.
33cba68c15: Symptoms. On a Monday morning, the cost dashboard for the order-status assistant shows input tokens per day up about sixfold. Customers complain that the assistant "thinks for a long time and then says it can't help". The median turns per run is normally 3. Now it's 10, the configured maximum. No prompt or model change was deployed.
36b22dacab:
Trace evidence. Run the six-pass protocol from section 14 on one affected run (the abridged trace is shown there).

  • Pass 1: ten tool_use turns, no end_turn, outcome stopped:max_turns.
  • Pass 2: the first get_orders result is is_error: true with the five-character body error, returned in about 40 ms.
  • Pass 3: ten identical calls with {"customer_id": "C-7"}.
  • Pass 5: input tokens grow by a constant amount per turn, consistent with the loop and nothing else.

Every affected run has the same shape. Runs that don't call get_orders are normal.
44ca5f61c3:
Isolation step. The question is whether the model is misbehaving, or responding sensibly to what it's given.

Call get_orders directly from a test harness with the recorded input. It fails every time, so the tool failure is deterministic and independent of the model. The tool's own log has the real exception. The order service, upgraded to v3 over the weekend, rejects the field cust_id and expects customerId.

Then look at the model's side. It got the result "error" with no explanation. The tool-handling docs say what it does with an invalid call: it retries with corrections. With no information to correct, it retries the same call. The model's behaviour is reasonable for its input. The defect is entirely in the integration layer, in two places.
4d7ef6353d:
Root cause. First, a contract change in a downstream API broke the tool adapter, and no contract test caught it. Second, the dispatcher's generic except Exception: return "error" erased the kind of failure. The model couldn't tell a permanent fault from a transient one, and nothing in code limited repeated identical failures.

The first defect took the feature down. The second turned that into a cost incident and a bad user experience.
ecc7a61254:
Fix. Immediately: fix the adapter's field name. Structurally, three changes:

  • Classify exceptions in the dispatcher. Return a structured error with retryable: false and a next-step hint ("tell the user orders cannot be checked now; do not say they have no orders"). Keep the raw exception in the internal log only.
  • Add the identical-failure guard from section 08, which stops the third identical failing call.
  • Add a contract test against the order service's published schema to the CI pipeline.

Example 23 shows the run going from ten turns to two, with an honest answer. It also shows the guard stopping a model that ignores retryable: false on the third call.

Guards: alert on tool error rate by tool (section 13), on p95 turns per run, and on the share of runs ending in stopped:max_turns.
fc25203ccf:
Symptoms. A ticket-routing service classifies each inbound message into billing, outage or cancel. The team moves it from an older model to claude-opus-5-5. In staging, every request immediately fails with HTTP 400. A developer removes the line that looked unusual, and the 400s stop.

In production, about 18% of messages then fail with JSONDecodeError and land in a manual queue. The incident channel's first theory is "the new model is worse at JSON".
f1b032cfad:
Trace evidence. Before forming a theory, read three things.

First, the 400 body in staging. It's an invalid_request_error about a prefilled assistant message. The errors page lists exactly this among common validation errors: Claude 4.6+ models reject a prefilled final assistant message. The old code had sent {"role": "assistant", "content": "{"} as the last message, a once-common trick to force bare JSON, and parsed "{" + text. The developer's hot-fix removed that message.

Second, the failing production responses. They show stop_reason: end_turn and HTTP 200. The text begins either with a fence (```json) or with a sentence ("Here is the classification:") before a valid object.

Third, the rendered-request diff between old and new versions. The prefill message is gone, and nothing else about the format instruction changed.
8dcc5d12fd:
Isolation step. Replay the recorded failing responses through the current parser. They fail every time, so the parser is deterministic, and the responses themselves aren't bare JSON. That leaves a model-output question: the new model, without the prefill, sometimes wraps its JSON.

Repeating 200 representative inputs gives 36 failures (example 24), a measured rate of 18%. All of them are JSONDecodeError; none are truncated or refused. So the model isn't "worse at JSON". Every failing response contains a valid object. The real problem is that the integration relied on a technique the new model doesn't accept. The hot-fix removed the technique without replacing the guarantee it gave.
2e3406fa47: Root cause.
