Three things together: an integration dependency on prefill, a parser that assumed bare JSON, and a model upgrade done without first running the output contract against the new model. The 400 and the parse failures are both integration consequences of a model change. Neither is the model "getting worse".
ae2277974f:
Fix. Replace the prefill with structured outputs: output_config.format with type: "json_schema" and the enum in the schema, per the structured-outputs page. (The older output_format parameter is deprecated and needs a beta header. The Python SDK's messages.parse helper sends the new form for you.) Example 24 goes from 36 failures in 200 to none.

Keep the parser strict, and have it check stop_reason first. The same page says refusals and max_tokens responses may not match the schema.

Read the page's limitations before you move the schema over:

  • numeric and string-length constraints such as minimum and maxLength aren't supported and return a 400;
  • additionalProperties must be false;
  • structured outputs are incompatible with citations and with prefill;
  • enum values can come back with different capitalisation, so compare enums case-insensitively and avoid values that differ only in case.

Guard: a pre-upgrade gate that runs the recorded input set against the candidate model in shadow, and compares parse rate and accuracy before the switch (chapter 15). Add a parse-failure-rate alert per journey.
dcda0b340f: A regex that strips code fences would also have made the 18% pass, and at 02:00 it's tempting. Treat it as a temporary mitigation with a metric attached, not as the fix. It handles the two wrappers seen so far. It says nothing about the next one. And it hides the fact that nothing enforces the output contract any more.
3c1e2a2e52:
Across the three cases, the pattern is the chapter's thesis in practice. Each incident arrived with a model-shaped theory. Each was settled by a cheap deterministic step: timestamps, a direct tool call, a replay and an error body. And each root cause was in code or configuration you own.

That's not because the model never fails. It's because integration failures are more common, cheaper to find, and more often blamed on the model.
e132b4e9fe: Each anti-pattern below passes code review, because it looks like error handling. The broken version comes first, then the fix, then the failure it causes in one line. Several appeared in earlier sections. They're collected here because a reviewer needs them in one place.
26ff8e8c48: Failure caused: runaway cost on inputs that don't contain the required data. Repeated guesses then eventually pass validation with invented values.
4a154e887a: Failure caused: customer phone numbers and account ids end up in a log index everyone can search. And the log bill grows with the square of conversation length.
67910bec20: Failure caused: the symptom moves (the model now says "I could not find your orders, please call"). The root cause, an opaque tool error, stays in place and corrupts other answers.
4b7cba7836: Broken: "I set temperature to 0, reran the request, it worked, closing the ticket." Fixed: replay the recorded response to settle the integration question. Then repeat the rendered request N times, and compare rates before and after the fix. Failure caused: on the newest models the request is rejected outright (chapter 05). On others, a single clean run says almost nothing about a 5% failure (section 16).
230e6f5d19: Failure caused: a model call fails on turn 3, the step restarts, turn 1 runs again, and a second incident ticket gets opened. The Messages API call has no side effects. The agent step does.
06037609f0: Failure caused: nothing enforces the output contract, and the next wrapper variant breaks parsing again. Meanwhile the patch hides the parse-failure rate that would have warned you (case study C).
0b5a8bf888:
Every debugged failure should leave two artefacts behind.

For an integration bug, that's a unit test. It replays the recording, or scripts the fake to produce the failing condition (truncated response, 400, empty tool result), and asserts the fixed behaviour. It runs in milliseconds in CI, forever.

For a model-output issue, it's a case in the evaluation set: the input, plus the expected tool or a grader for the output. It runs against every prompt or model change, and you track the failure rate over time. Evaluation design itself belongs to chapter 04 and the professional exam. Here it's the regression net every fix lands in.
440936c4ee:
Test the error paths, not only the happy path. The tests a reviewer should ask for are short (example 15):

  • a 400 is never retried;
  • a spend-cap 429 is not treated as capacity;
  • truncated JSON is never parsed;
  • the breaker ignores 4xx;
  • fallback does not hide a 401;
  • repair is bounded;
  • a clean request passes the invariant checks.

With the fake client, each is three to five lines. A Spring team writes the same set with JUnit and WireMock scenarios.
8bb530bec5: The first wrong record in the trace is the tool result. It's an error with no explanation, and it can't be told apart from "no data". That's an integration defect. A bigger model (A) receives the same uninformative result. A prompt rule (B) treats the symptom, and may produce a different wrong answer. D is unrelated.
824e7c97df: Stacked retries multiply load. Fixed sleeps synchronise it. And with no breaker, every request spends its whole budget waiting. B fixes all three. A and D add load during overload. C changes the product's latency contract, and it's right only for work that can wait.
